explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The writer says, “This is the message you have heard from the beginning: We should love one another.” It isn't a fresh idea they're hearing for the first time. They've had it since the start, and they still get to practice it today.

Fasting and praying don't show up in this verse, friend. The message from the beginning is “We should love one another.” I'd love for the answer to be a nice long to-do list, but the writer keeps it short and puts love right up front.

Going and preaching isn't what the writer names here, friend. The verse says, “We should love one another.” That's the whole message, and it's sitting right there in the open like a fresh batch on the cooling rack.

Evil goes in the first blank. The writer says Cain's own deeds were evil. Cain, Adam and Eve's son (Genesis 4:1), belonged to the evil one and murdered his brother. It's a heavy verse, so I'll just say it plainly and let it sit.

Righteous goes in the second blank. That's the writer's word for the deeds of Cain's brother. I think this part of the verse hurts to read, friend, because the brother's deeds were righteous and Cain killed him anyway.

Secret sounds dramatic, but it isn't in this verse. The writer says Cain's own deeds were evil and his brother's were righteous. Nothing here is about who knew what or who hid what. Stick with the words the writer actually gives us.

Nobody's deeds are called praised in this verse, friend. The writer says Cain's were evil and his brother's were righteous. Those two words carry the whole sentence, and the verse doesn't say whether anyone clapped for anybody.
I know a thing or two about forgotten, friend, but it's not the word here. The writer says Cain's own deeds were evil and his brother's were righteous. That's the pair that fits both blanks.

The writer says the opposite, friend. He tells his brothers, “So do not be surprised, brothers, if the world hates you.” He's not telling them to expect applause. He's giving them a heads-up so they aren't caught off guard.

That's right, friend. The writer says, “So do not be surprised, brothers, if the world hates you.” He doesn't tell them the world will love them. He tells them not to be surprised if it hates them. A heads-up like that beats getting caught off guard.

Love is the word, friend. The writer says, “We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love our brothers.” It's how we know. Not a feeling we hope is true, but love showing up toward our brothers.

Correcting isn't what the writer points to here. He says we know we have passed from death to life “…because we love our brothers.” I've corrected a lot of crooked cookie edges in my day, but that's not how this verse measures it.

Teaching is a fine job, friend, but it's not the word in this verse. The writer says we know we have passed from death to life “…because we love our brothers.” Love is what he names, and he names it plainly.
That's the word, friend. The writer says, “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer…” It's a strong thing to say, and he says it plainly. He adds that eternal life does not reside in a murderer.

Thief isn't the word the writer uses here. He says, “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer…” That's a heavy line, so I'll just keep to what the verse says. It's about hating a brother, and the writer's word for it is murderer.

Coward isn't in this verse, friend. The writer says, “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer…” That's the name he gives. I think it's a hard verse, and it's meant to make us stop and take it seriously.

explanations.answer: Jesus laid down His life for us
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The writer says, “By this we know what love is: Jesus laid down His life for us…” He doesn't point to a definition. He points to what Jesus did. Then he says we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers.

explanations.answer: Jesus wrote it on stone tablets
explanations.explanation: Stone tablets aren't in this verse, friend. The writer says, “By this we know what love is: Jesus laid down His life for us…” Love is shown by what Jesus did for us, and that's where the writer sends us to look.

explanations.answer: Jesus showed it to us in a vision
explanations.explanation: No vision here, friend. The writer says, “By this we know what love is: Jesus laid down His life for us…” That's the answer he gives. He goes straight to what Jesus did for us.

True, friend. The writer says, “…we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers.” He says it right after pointing to Jesus laying down His life for us. It's a big ask, and the writer says it straight.
The writer actually says this, friend. His words are, “…we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers.” It comes right after he says Jesus laid down His life for us. So the statement is true.

explanations.answer: How can the love of God abide in him
explanations.explanation: That's his question, friend. The writer asks, “…how can the love of God abide in him?” He's talking about the one who has earthly possessions, sees his brother in need and withholds his compassion. He lets the question hang there on purpose, I think, and it's a good one to chew on.

explanations.answer: Why didn't his brother ask sooner
explanations.explanation: The writer never asks that, friend. His question is about the one who has earthly possessions and withholds his compassion: “…how can the love of God abide in him?” He puts the spotlight on the person who sees the need. Nothing in the verse blames the brother for waiting.

explanations.answer: Who will pay his brother back
explanations.explanation: Paying back isn't in this verse, friend. The writer asks, “…how can the love of God abide in him?” He says it about the person who sees his brother in need and withholds his compassion. No ledger, no tab, just that question.
That's it, friend. The writer says, “Little children, let us love not in word and speech, but in action and truth.” Love that shows up and does something. That kind of love doesn't need a speech.

That's the one the writer says to set aside, friend. He says, “…let us love not in word and speech, but in action and truth.” Words and speech are fine as far as they go. But he wants love to be backed by action and truth.

Feeling and thought aren't the pair in this verse, friend. The writer says, “…let us love not in word and speech, but in action and truth.” He's looking for love you can see in action. A warm thought on its own doesn't carry a box across the room.

The writer says something different, friend. He says, “And by this we will know that we belong to the truth…” It's the truth, not the world. He says it right after telling his little children to love in action and truth. The world doesn't show up in that line at all.
Right, friend. The writer says, “And by this we will know that we belong to the truth…” Not the world, the truth. It comes right after he tells his little children to love in action and truth.

explanations.answer: God is greater than our hearts
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The writer says, “Even if our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts, and He knows all things.” Our hearts can be loud, but they don't get the last word. God is greater.

That's not what the writer says, friend. He says, “Even if our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts…” He doesn't say God agrees with a condemning heart. He says God is greater than our hearts. He adds that God “…knows all things.”

explanations.answer: God stays far from our hearts
explanations.explanation: The writer doesn't say that, friend. He says, “Even if our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts, and He knows all things.” Nothing in that line puts God far away. He is greater than our hearts and knows all things.
The writer says the opposite, friend. He says, “Beloved, if our hearts do not condemn us, we have confidence before God…” Confidence, not fear. That's the very thing he names.
That's right, friend. The writer says, “Beloved, if our hearts do not condemn us, we have confidence before God…” He doesn't say we should still be afraid. He says we have confidence.

explanations.answer: We keep His commandments and do what pleases Him
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the writer gives, friend. He says we will receive from God whatever we ask, “…because we keep His commandments and do what is pleasing in His sight.” Both parts are in the verse.

explanations.answer: We ask Him again and again until He says yes
explanations.explanation: That's not the reason the writer gives, friend. He says we receive whatever we ask “…because we keep His commandments and do what is pleasing in His sight.” Nothing in the verse is about asking over and over until the answer changes.

explanations.answer: We give Him a tenth of everything we earn
explanations.explanation: Giving a tenth isn't the reason in this verse, friend. The writer says we receive whatever we ask “…because we keep His commandments and do what is pleasing in His sight.” That's the reason he gives, and he gives it plainly.

True, friend. The writer says, “And this is His commandment: that we should believe in the name of His Son, Jesus Christ…” Then he adds that we should love one another just as He commanded us. Two parts, one commandment.

The writer actually says this, friend. His words are, “And this is His commandment: that we should believe in the name of His Son, Jesus Christ…” Then he adds loving one another. So believing in the name of His Son is part one, and the statement is true.

explanations.answer: By the Spirit God has given us
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. The writer says, “And by this we know that He remains in us: by the Spirit He has given us.” The Spirit is a gift God gave, and that's how we know. I spent years in a junk drawer wondering if anybody remembered me, so I can tell you a gift like that means a lot.

explanations.answer: By the signs God shows us each day
explanations.explanation: Daily signs aren't what the writer names, friend. He says, “And by this we know that He remains in us: by the Spirit He has given us.” The answer is the Spirit. You don't have to go hunting for a sign when the verse hands you the answer.

explanations.answer: By the dreams God gives us at night
explanations.explanation: Dreams don't show up in this verse, friend. The writer says, “And by this we know that He remains in us: by the Spirit He has given us.” The answer is the Spirit God has given us. Nobody has to wait for bedtime to find out. Your pillow can take the night off.
